bio_ocrb.0.0.summary: These revision notes provide a comprehensive, Grade 9 level breakdown of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cellular genetic material and the required practical (PAG1) for observing cells under a light microscope. Every syllabus requirement for OCR GCSE Biology B B1.1 is covered in meticulous detail, including cellular structures, microscope calculations, magnification formulas, and staining techniques. Master these concepts to secure top marks in your GCSE exams.

core.h: Overview of Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells
core.p: All living organisms are composed of cells, which are broadly categorized into two types: eukaryotic and prokaryotic. Understanding their structural differences, particularly regarding genetic material, is fundamental to cellular biology and genetics.
bullets: Eukaryotic cells include plant, animal, and fungal cells and contain a distinct, membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells include bacteria and lack a true membrane-bound nucleus.
In eukaryotes, genetic material (DNA) is linear and organized into chromosomes packaged with histone proteins.
In prokaryotic cells, DNA is a single, circular loop found free in the cytoplasm, often accompanied by smaller rings of DNA called plasmids.

callouts.p: An organism whose cells contain a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
Bacteria do not have a nucleus; their main DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid.

core.h: Structure and Function of the Eukaryotic Nucleus
core.p: The nucleus is the control center of a eukaryotic cell, housing the organism's genome and orchestrating all cellular activities by regulating gene expression.
bullets: Surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which protects fragile DNA.
Contains nuclear pores that allow mRNA and ribosomes to pass out into the cytoplasm.
Contains nucleoplasm, a thick liquid substance that suspends chromatin.
Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes during cell division.
The nucleolus inside synthesizes ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

callouts.p: A double membrane perforated with pores that encloses the genetic material in eukaryotic cells.

core.p: Prokaryotes have a streamlined genetic layout suited for rapid reproduction through binary fission.
bullets: Main genetic material is a single circular double-stranded DNA molecule.
Found freely in the cytoplasm in an irregular region known as the nucleoid.
Plasmids are small, circular DNA molecules carrying extra genes (e.g., antibiotic resistance).
Plasmids can replicate independently of the main bacterial chromosome.
Prokaryotes lack histone proteins associated with their DNA.

callouts.p: Do not state that all prokaryotes have plasmids; they are common in bacteria but not universally present in every single prokaryotic species.

core.p: Light microscopes use light and glass lenses to form magnified images of biological specimens. They are essential tools for studying cellular structures in school laboratories.
bullets: Light passes through a thin specimen and through objective and eyepiece lenses.
Maximum useful magnification of a standard light microscope is usually around x1500.
Resolution is limited by the wavelength of light (approx. 200 nm).
Living or stained dead cells can be observed.
Inexpensive and easy to use compared to electron microscopes.

callouts.p: The shortest distance between two separate points in a microscope field that can still be distinguished as distinct entities.

core.h: Required Practical 1: Observing Plant and Animal Cells
core.p: PAG1 requires students to prepare temporary mounts of plant and animal cells and examine them using a light microscope, applying staining techniques to make internal structures visible.
bullets: Plant cell specimen: Onion epidermal peel or leaf epidermis.
Animal cell specimen: Human cheek epithelial cells scraped gently with a cotton bud.
Stain for plant cells: Iodine solution (or methylene blue) to stain starch and nuclei.
Stain for animal cells: Methylene blue to make colorless nuclei clearly visible.
Always use a coverslip lowered at an angle with a mounting needle to prevent air bubbles.

callouts.p: Air bubbles under a coverslip look like thick dark rings with bright centers under a microscope. Lowering the coverslip at 45 degrees prevents them.

core.p: Executing PAG1 safely and effectively requires a precise sequence of steps to ensure clear visualization of cellular structures.
bullets: 1. Place a drop of stain (e.g., iodine or methylene blue) onto the center of a clean glass microscope slide.
2. Use forceps to peel a thin layer of onion epidermis (or smear cheek cells) and place it flat in the stain.
3. Gently lower a coverslip onto the specimen at a 45-degree angle using a mounting needle to avoid trapping air bubbles.
4. Place the slide on the microscope stage and clip it securely in place.
5. Select the lowest power objective lens (e.g., x4) and use the coarse adjustment knob to bring the stage up until the specimen is roughly in view.
6. Use the fine adjustment knob to sharply focus the image.
7. Switch to higher power objective lenses (e.g., x10 or x40) for detailed cellular study, only using the fine adjustment knob.

callouts.p: Never use the coarse adjustment knob when using high power objective lenses, as you may drive the lens straight through the glass slide.

core.p: Biologists must be able to calculate magnification, image size, and actual size using standard scientific formulas and unit conversions.
bullets: The formula triangle is: Image Size = Magnification x Actual Size (I = A x M).
Rearranged for Magnification: M = Image Size / Actual Size.
Rearranged for Actual Size: A = Image Size / Magnification.
Units must always match before calculating (convert everything to micrometers or millimeters).
Standard unit conversions: 1 mm = 1000 µm.

callouts.p: How many times larger an image is compared to the actual size of the specimen.

core.p: Working through standard examination problems involving magnification requires strict adherence to formula selection and unit conversions.
bullets: Identify what values are given in the question (Image size and Actual size).
Check that both measurements are in the same units.
Substitute the numbers into the equation M = I / A.
State the final answer with a multiplication symbol (e.g., x400) and no units.

callouts.p: Magnification has no units because it is a ratio of two lengths measured in the same units.

core.h: Field of View and Scale Bars
core.p: When viewing specimens under a microscope, scale bars and estimates of cell size provide crucial quantitative context.
bullets: A scale bar represents a known actual length at a specific magnification.
To estimate cell size, divide the diameter of the field of view by the number of cells spanning across it.
Calibrated graticules in the eyepiece allow exact measurements of microscopic objects.
Drawing biological diagrams requires clear, continuous pencil lines with no shading.

callouts.p: Always use a sharp HB pencil, draw clear unbroken lines, do not shade, and include a total magnification label on your biological drawing.

core.p: While light microscopes are accessible and useful, their physical properties impose strict limits on what details can be observed inside cells.
bullets: Maximum magnification is typically limited to x1500 before the image becomes blurry (empty magnification).
Resolution is limited by the wavelength of visible light (approx. 400 - 700 nm).
Sub-cellular structures smaller than 200 nm (such as ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, or plasmids) cannot be resolved with a light microscope.
Electron microscopes must be used to view ultra-fine structures (organelles) due to their much smaller electron wavelength.

callouts.p: A microscope that uses a beam of electrons instead of light to achieve much higher magnification and resolution.

analogy.t: The Library and the Archival Vault
analogy.p: Imagine a eukaryotic cell as a massive national library. The nucleus is the secure, climate-controlled archival vault in the center where the master recipe books (linear DNA chromosomes) are locked away safely behind thick doors (nuclear envelope) with guarded slot dropboxes (nuclear pores) allowing copied recipes (mRNA) out to the kitchen staff (ribosomes). In contrast, a prokaryotic cell is like a cosy neighborhood bakery where the single main recipe scroll sits unbound right on the kitchen table in the open air (nucleoid), along with a few loose laminated recipe cards for quick tips (plasmids). This analogy breaks down because bacterial DNA is actually supercoiled and organized by proteins rather than floating in complete total disorder like loose papers.

terms.d: A cell that possesses a true membrane-bound nucleus and linear chromosomes.
A cell that lacks a membrane-bound nucleus, with free circular DNA in the cytoplasm.
The membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains genetic material.
A small circular loop of DNA found in bacterial cells carrying extra non-essential genes.
The region in a prokaryotic cell where the single circular DNA molecule is located.
A double membrane perforated with pores that surrounds the eukaryotic nucleus.
The number of times larger an image is compared to the actual specimen size.
The ability to distinguish between two distinct points that are very close together.
A stain used in microscopy to make animal cell nuclei clearly visible.
A stain used in plant cell microscopy to highlight starch grains and nuclei.
A thin piece of glass placed over a specimen on a microscope slide.
The circular area visible through the microscope eyepiece lens.

mistakes.w: Saying bacteria have a nucleus.
mistakes.r: Bacteria are prokaryotes and have no true nucleus; their DNA is in a nucleoid region.

mistakes.w: Stating magnification has units like mm or µm.
mistakes.r: Magnification is a ratio and has no units (written as x400).

mistakes.w: Using the coarse adjustment knob on high power.
mistakes.r: Only use the fine adjustment knob on high power to avoid breaking slides and lenses.

mistakes.w: Placing the coverslip straight down onto a slide.
mistakes.r: Lower the coverslip at a 45-degree angle using a needle to prevent air bubbles.

mistakes.w: Confusing resolution with magnification.
mistakes.r: Magnification is size increase; resolution is clarity and detail between close points.

mistakes.w: Describing eukaryotic DNA as circular.
mistakes.r: Eukaryotic DNA is linear; only prokaryotic and mitochondrial/chloroplast DNA is circular.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert units before calculating magnification.
mistakes.r: Always ensure image and actual size use the same unit (e.g., both in µm).

exam.q: State two differences between the genetic material of a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell.
model: Eukaryotic DNA is linear / Prokaryotic DNA is circular
Eukaryotic DNA is enclosed in a nucleus / Prokaryotic DNA is in the cytoplasm / nucleoid
Eukaryotic DNA is associated with histones / Prokaryotic DNA is not
exam.tip: Mention two clear structural differences without mixing up plant and bacterial features.

exam.q: Calculate the actual width of a cell image if it measures 45 mm under a microscope at x300 magnification. Give your answer in micrometers.
model: Convert image size to micrometers: 45 mm x 1000 = 45000 µm
Recall formula: Actual size = Image size / Magnification
Calculation: 45000 / 300 = 150 µm
exam.tip: Always convert units first before performing division to avoid order of magnitude errors.

exam.q: Describe the function of nuclear pores in a eukaryotic cell.
model: Allow molecules to move between the nucleus and cytoplasm
Examples include mRNA leaving the nucleus or proteins entering
exam.tip: Keep it specific: nuclear pores control traffic across the nuclear envelope.

exam.q: Explain why a student must lower the coverslip at an angle during slide preparation in PAG1.
model: To prevent trapping air bubbles
Air bubbles obstruct the view of the cells under the microscope
exam.tip: Reference both the method (angle) and the problem it avoids (air bubbles).

exam.q: A student views an onion cell with a light microscope. State why they cannot see ribosomes inside the cell.
model: Ribosomes are smaller than the resolution limit of a light microscope
Ribosomes are smaller than 200 nm / light wavelength is too large
exam.tip: Link the failure to see ribosomes directly to resolution limits, not magnification.

exam.q: Give the formula linking image size, actual size, and magnification.
model: Magnification = Image size / Actual size (or equivalent triangle rearrangement)
exam.tip: Write the formula clearly; any standard variation is accepted if mathematically correct.

exam.q: Describe the role of plasmids in prokaryotic cells.
model: Carry extra genes
Such as antibiotic resistance genes that can be shared between bacteria
exam.tip: Emphasize that plasmids are separate from the main chromosome and carry non-essential adaptive genes.

exam.q: Explain why methylene blue is added when preparing a cheek cell slide.
model: To stain cellular structures / nuclei
Makes transparent structures visible against the bright background
exam.tip: Cheek cells are mostly transparent; stains provide contrast.

exam.q: Compare the size of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
model: Eukaryotic cells are larger (10 - 100 µm)
Prokaryotic cells are smaller (1 - 5 µm)
exam.tip: Include approximate size ranges to secure both marks easily.

exam.q: State one advantage of a light microscope over an electron microscope.
model: Cheaper to purchase and maintain / Can view living cells / Portable / Easy to prepare
exam.tip: Remember that light microscopes allow viewing of live specimens, unlike electron microscopes.

exam.q: Describe how to safely focus on a specimen using a light microscope starting from low power.
model: Place slide on stage and select lowest power objective lens
Use coarse adjustment knob to bring stage up (or lens down) until in rough focus
Use fine adjustment knob to sharpen the image before switching to higher power
exam.tip: Always specify starting on low power and using the coarse knob cautiously.

worked.q: An image of a plant cell is 60 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 50 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
steps: Step 1: Convert image size from millimeters to micrometers. 60 mm x 1000 = 60000 µm.
Step 2: State the magnification formula: Magnification = Image size / Actual size.
Step 3: Substitute the numbers: Magnification = 60000 / 50.
Step 4: Calculate the final value: 1200.

worked.q: A bacterium has an actual length of 2 µm. It is drawn with a length of 80 mm in a textbook diagram. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
steps: Step 1: Convert image size to micrometers: 80 mm x 1000 = 80000 µm.
Step 2: Recall the formula: Magnification = Image size / Actual size.
Step 3: Substitute values: 80000 / 2.
Step 4: Compute the result.

bio_ocrb.0.3.summary: These comprehensive revision notes cover DNA nucleotides, the triplet code, and protein synthesis involving mRNA and ribosomes for OCR GCSE Biology B (Twenty First Century Science). They detail the exact molecular structure of nucleotides, the transcription of genetic code from DNA to mRNA in the nucleus, and the translation of mRNA into polypeptide chains at the ribosome. Designed for Grade 9 mastery, the notes incorporate complete diagrams, precise mark-scheme definitions, common student misconceptions, and fully worked exam questions.

core.p: DNA is a polymer made up of repeating units called nucleotides. Each individual nucleotide consists of three distinct chemical components: a pentose sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and an organic nitrogen-containing base. These building blocks link together via strong chemical bonds to form the iconic double-helix polymer structure.
bullets: A nucleotide is composed of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base.
The sugar in DNA is always deoxyribose.
The phosphate group is attached to the sugar molecule.
The base is attached to the sugar and can be one of four types: Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine, or Guanine.
Nucleotides join together to form long polynucleotide strands.

callouts.p: The monomer of DNA, consisting of a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
The alternating sugar and phosphate molecules form a strong structural backbone for each DNA strand.

core.p: The two strands of a DNA molecule are held together by hydrogen bonds formed between specific pairs of nitrogenous bases. This precise pairing mechanism ensures that the genetic code is accurately copied and maintained across generations.
bullets: Adenine (A) always pairs exclusively with Thymine (T).
Cytosine (C) always pairs exclusively with Guanine (G).
This rule is known as complementary base pairing.
Base pairs are held together by weak hydrogen bonds.
The two strands run antiparallel to each other, twisting into a double helix.

callouts.p: A always pairs with T; C always pairs with G. Remember: Apples on Trees, Cars in Garages.
Do not confuse complementary base pairing with covalent bonding of the backbone; bases pair via hydrogen bonds.

core.p: The genetic instructions stored within DNA are encoded as a sequence of bases. A sequence of three adjacent bases on a DNA strand is called a triplet. Each triplet codes for a specific amino acid in a protein chain.
bullets: Three bases make up one triplet.
Each triplet codes for one specific amino acid.
The order of triplets determines the exact order of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Proteins are polymers constructed from chains of amino acids.
There are 64 possible triplet combinations using 4 different bases.

callouts.p: A sequence of three DNA bases that specifies a particular amino acid to be included in a protein.
Always state that a triplet codes for an amino acid, not a whole protein directly.

core.h: 4. The Role of the Nucleus in Protein Synthesis
core.p: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus through the nuclear pores. Therefore, its genetic instructions must be copied into a smaller, movable molecule that can travel to the site of protein synthesis in the cytoplasm.
bullets: DNA remains securely inside the nucleus to prevent damage.
Protein synthesis takes place on ribosomes located in the cytoplasm.
An intermediary molecule, messenger RNA (mRNA), is required to transport the code.
The first step of protein synthesis involves making an mRNA copy of a gene.
This process is known as transcription.

callouts.p: DNA cannot fit through nuclear pores; mRNA is small enough to pass through them.
Never say DNA leaves the nucleus during protein synthesis.

core.p: Transcription is the process by which the genetic code for a specific protein is copied from a DNA strand into a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule. This occurs inside the nucleus before translation can begin.
bullets: The DNA double helix unzips around the gene to be expressed.
Free RNA nucleotides pair up with complementary bases on the template DNA strand.
Note that in RNA, Uracil (U) replaces Thymine (T) and pairs with Adenine (A).
An enzyme called RNA polymerase joins the RNA nucleotides together to form an mRNA strand.
The completed mRNA molecule detaches and leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore.

callouts.p: The synthesis of an mRNA molecule from a DNA template strand inside the nucleus.
RNA contains Uracil (U) instead of Thymine (T); U pairs with A.

core.p: Ribosomes are cellular structures composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins. They act as the workbench where the genetic code carried by mRNA is translated into an amino acid sequence.
bullets: Ribosomes are found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
They bind to the mRNA molecule once it arrives from the nucleus.
Ribosomes move along the mRNA molecule three bases at a time.
They catalyse the formation of peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids.
Ribosomes ensure the correct order of amino acids matches the genetic code.

callouts.p: A cell organelle that translates mRNA into a polypeptide chain during protein synthesis.
Mention both transcription (nucleus) and translation (ribosome) for full marks on protein synthesis.

core.p: Translation is the second major stage of protein synthesis. During translation, the sequence of bases on the mRNA is read by the ribosome in groups of three, known as codons, to assemble a specific protein.
bullets: An mRNA triplet is called a codon.
The ribosome reads the mRNA codons sequentially.
Molecules of tRNA bring specific amino acids to the ribosome, matching their anticodon to the mRNA codon.
Amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide chain.
Once completed, the polypeptide folds into a specific 3D shape to become a functional protein.

callouts.p: The process at the ribosome where the genetic code in mRNA is translated into a sequence of amino acids.
A triplet is on DNA; a codon is the complementary group of three bases on mRNA.

core.p: The genetic code exhibits specific universal properties that ensure accurate translation across almost all living organisms.
bullets: The code is a triplet code (3 bases per amino acid).
It is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet.
It is non-overlapping, meaning each base is read only once as part of one triplet.
It is universal, meaning the same triplets code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.
There are specific start and stop codons that signal the beginning and end of protein synthesis.

callouts.p: A genetic code where multiple codons can code for the same single amino acid.
All organisms share the same basic genetic code, providing evidence for evolution.

core.h: 9. Relationship Between DNA, Proteins, and Phenotype
core.p: The sequence of bases in DNA ultimately determines the phenotype of an organism by controlling the production of functional proteins such as enzymes, structural proteins, and hormones.
bullets: DNA stores genetic instructions in the base sequence.
Transcription produces mRNA from the DNA code.
Translation produces a polypeptide chain at the ribosome.
Polypeptides fold into specific 3D protein structures (e.g., enzymes, structural proteins).
Proteins determine cellular activities and physical traits, constituting the organism's phenotype.

callouts.p: The observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its genotype and environmental interactions.
Clearly link DNA base sequence to amino acid sequence to protein shape to phenotype.

core.p: Although both DNA and RNA are nucleic acids involved in genetic information storage and protein synthesis, they possess distinct structural and chemical differences.
bullets: DNA is double-stranded; RNA is single-stranded.
DNA contains deoxyribose sugar; RNA contains ribose sugar.
DNA contains Thymine (T); RNA contains Uracil (U).
DNA is found mainly in the nucleus; RNA functions in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
DNA is stable for long-term storage; RNA is relatively short-lived.

callouts.p: RNA has Uracil instead of Thymine and ribose instead of deoxyribose.

core.p: Changes in the base sequence of DNA, known as mutations, can alter the amino acid sequence of a protein, potentially affecting its 3D shape and biological function.
bullets: A mutation is a random change in the base sequence of DNA.
Substitution, insertion, or deletion of bases can change DNA triplets.
Changed triplets result in altered mRNA codons during transcription.
Altered codons may introduce different amino acids during translation.
If the protein's shape changes significantly (e.g., an enzyme's active site), its function may be lost.

callouts.p: A random change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA that can result in altered proteins.
Not all mutations change the amino acid sequence due to the degenerate nature of the genetic code.

core.p: Protein synthesis is a two-stage sequential process connecting nuclear DNA instructions with cytoplasmic protein production.
bullets: Stage 1: Transcription. DNA unwinds; mRNA is synthesized using complementary base pairing in the nucleus.
mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore and travels to a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
Stage 2: Translation. Ribosome reads mRNA codons.
tRNA molecules bring amino acids corresponding to each codon.
Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide chain.

callouts.p: Transcription in the nucleus followed by Translation at the ribosome.
Always state the location (nucleus vs cytoplasm/ribosome) for each stage of protein synthesis.

analogy.p:
Imagine DNA as a priceless master recipe book locked securely in the library safe (the nucleus). Because the head chef cannot risk the original book getting stained or lost in the bustling kitchen, a photocopy of a single recipe is made (transcription of mRNA). This photocopy is then carried out of the office into the kitchen workstation (the ribosome), where junior chefs read the instructions and assemble the ingredients (amino acids) into a finished dish (a protein). 

Where it breaks down: A recipe book is written in human language and photocopied identically letter-for-letter, whereas transcription converts DNA base language into RNA base language using complementary pairing (including replacing Thymine with Uracil).

terms.d: The monomer of nucleic acids, consisting of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
A double-helix polymer of nucleotides that stores genetic information in cells.
The specific pairing of bases: A with T (or U in RNA), and C with G.
A sequence of three DNA bases that codes for one amino acid.
A sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for an amino acid.
The synthesis of an mRNA molecule from a DNA template strand inside the nucleus.
The process at the ribosome where mRNA is translated into an amino acid sequence.
Messenger RNA, a single-stranded molecule that carries genetic code from DNA to the ribosome.
A cell organelle where protein synthesis (translation) takes place.
The monomer building block of proteins.
A polymer chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA.
A nitrogenous base found in RNA that replaces thymine and pairs with adenine.
The pentose sugar found in DNA nucleotides.
The observable characteristics of an organism resulting from genotype and environment.

mistakes.w: Saying DNA leaves the nucleus during protein synthesis.
mistakes.r: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus; only mRNA copies leave through nuclear pores.

mistakes.w: Stating that a triplet codes for a whole protein.
mistakes.r: A triplet (or codon) codes for a single amino acid, whereas a gene codes for a protein.

mistakes.w: Writing that Thymine pairs with Uracil in RNA.
mistakes.r: Adenine pairs with Uracil in RNA; Thymine is replaced by Uracil in RNA molecules.

mistakes.w: Confusing transcription and translation locations.
mistakes.r: Transcription happens in the nucleus; translation happens at the ribosome in the cytoplasm.

mistakes.w: Describing mRNA as double-stranded.
mistakes.r: mRNA is a single-stranded molecule.

mistakes.w: Calling amino acids the monomers of DNA.
mistakes.r: Amino acids are monomers of proteins; nucleotides are monomers of DNA.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that RNA contains ribose instead of deoxyribose.
mistakes.r: RNA contains ribose sugar, while DNA contains deoxyribose sugar.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a DNA nucleotide.
model: Consists of a phosphate group
Attached to a pentose sugar (deoxyribose)
And one of four nitrogenous bases (A, T, C, G)
exam.tip: Name all three components clearly for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why DNA remains inside the nucleus during protein synthesis.
model: DNA is too large to fit through the nuclear pores
Staying inside protects the genetic material from damage
exam.tip: Focus on molecular size and protection.

exam.q: State the role of mRNA in protein synthesis.
model: Carries the genetic code / instructions
From the DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome in the cytoplasm
exam.tip: Mention both origin (nucleus) and destination (ribosome).

exam.q: Explain what is meant by the term 'triplet code'.
model: A sequence of three bases on DNA
Cods for one specific amino acid
exam.tip: Ensure you link three bases to one amino acid.

exam.q: Compare the structure of DNA with the structure of RNA.
model: DNA is double-stranded whereas RNA is single-stranded
DNA contains deoxyribose sugar whereas RNA contains ribose sugar
DNA contains Thymine whereas RNA contains Uracil
DNA is found in the nucleus whereas RNA is found in nucleus and cytoplasm
exam.tip: Use comparative language (whereas, in contrast) and cover at least 4 differences.

exam.q: Describe how transcription produces an mRNA molecule.
model: DNA strands unzip around the gene
Free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases on the template strand (A with U, C with G)
RNA polymerase joins the RNA nucleotides together
Completed mRNA detaches and leaves the nucleus
exam.tip: Mention RNA polymerase and complementary base pairing.

exam.q: Describe what happens during translation at the ribosome.
model: Ribosome reads mRNA codons
tRNA brings specific amino acids matching the codons
Amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide
exam.tip: Keep the steps in logical chronological order.

exam.q: Explain how a mutation in the DNA base sequence can affect the phenotype of an organism.
model: A mutation changes the DNA base sequence
This alters the mRNA codon during transcription
Which may change the amino acid sequence during translation
Leading to a different protein structure and altered phenotype
exam.tip: Trace the causal chain from DNA to mRNA to amino acid to protein.

exam.q: If a section of DNA has 150 bases, calculate the maximum number of amino acids it can code for.
model: 150 bases / 3 bases per triplet = 50 triplets
Therefore it codes for a maximum of 50 amino acids
exam.tip: Divide the total number of bases by 3.

exam.q: Explain why the genetic code is described as degenerate.
model: Most amino acids are coded for
By more than one triplet / codon
exam.tip: State clearly that multiple codons specify the same amino acid.

worked.q: A gene on a DNA template strand has the base sequence: TAC GGC TTA. State the sequence of codons on the mRNA molecule produced by transcription of this gene.
steps: Identify that mRNA is synthesized using complementary base pairing with Uracil replacing Thymine.
Find the complementary mRNA base for each DNA base: A pairs with U, T pairs with A, C pairs with G, G pairs with C.
DNA triplet 1: TAC -> mRNA codon 1: AUG
DNA triplet 2: GGC -> mRNA codon 2: CCG
DNA triplet 3: TTA -> mRNA codon 3: AAU

worked.q: A polypeptide chain contains 120 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of DNA bases required in the gene coding for this polypeptide.
steps: Identify that each amino acid is coded by one triplet of bases.
Recall that each triplet consists of 3 bases.
Multiply the number of amino acids by 3: 120 x 3 = 360.

bio_ocrb.0.9.summary: This section explores how understanding the human genome transforms modern medicine through the identification of disease alleles and the application of genetic testing. Students must understand how specific gene variants lead to inherited conditions, how tests are conducted on embryos, fetuses, and adults, and evaluate the ethical implications of knowing one's genetic future.

core.p: A disease allele is a mutated version of a gene that causes or increases the risk of developing a genetic disorder. These alleles arise through mutations that alter the sequence of DNA bases, leading to faulty proteins or missing proteins.
bullets: Alleles are alternative forms of the same gene found at the same locus on a chromosome.
A disease allele can be recessive (requiring two copies for the disease phenotype) or dominant (requiring only one copy).
Examples include the cystic fibrosis allele (recessive) and the Huntington's disease allele (dominant).
Mutations in coding DNA change the amino acid sequence, altering the protein's 3D shape and function.

callouts.p: An alternative form of a gene whose variant DNA sequence leads to a faulty protein, causing a genetic disorder.

fig.cap: Comparing normal and disease alleles and their resultant proteins.

core.p: Genetic testing involves analysing a person's DNA or chromosomes to detect disease-associated alleles or gene variants. It can be used for diagnostic purposes, carrier testing, predictive testing, and prenatal screening.
bullets: DNA is typically extracted from white blood cells, mouth swabs, or amniotic fluid cells.
Techniques can look for specific single-gene mutations or broader chromosomal abnormalities.
It allows individuals to make informed reproductive choices or plan medical interventions.
Results carry significant psychological, social, and ethical implications.

callouts.p: Genetic tests look for DNA sequences that match known disease alleles to predict or diagnose inherited conditions.

core.h: 3. Types of Genetic Tests: Predictive and Diagnostic
core.p: Predictive testing is used to identify gene variants that increase a person's risk of developing diseases later in life, such as certain cancers or Huntington's disease, before symptoms appear. Diagnostic testing confirms whether a person has a suspected genetic condition when symptoms are already present.
bullets: Predictive testing helps in proactive monitoring and lifestyle changes.
Diagnostic testing provides a definitive answer for ongoing symptoms.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene testing assesses hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk.
A positive predictive test does not mean the disease will definitely develop with 100% certainty in all multi-factorial conditions.

callouts.p: Genetic testing carried out on healthy people with a family history of a genetic disorder to see if they carry a disease allele.

core.p: Prenatal testing checks an unborn fetus for genetic disorders using cells obtained from amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS). This allows parents to know if their baby has a condition before birth.
bullets: Amniocentesis involves taking a sample of amniotic fluid containing fetal cells at 15-20 weeks of pregnancy.
Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) involves taking a small sample of placental tissue at 11-14 weeks.
Both procedures carry a small risk of inducing miscarriage.
Results help parents prepare or make decisions about continuing the pregnancy.

callouts.p: Always remember that prenatal invasive tests like amniocentesis and CVS carry a risk of miscarriage, which is why they are only offered when there is a high risk of a serious genetic condition.

fig.cap: Overview of prenatal testing methods and timeframes.

core.p: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is performed on embryos created through In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) before they are implanted into the uterus. This ensures only embryos free of specific disease alleles are implanted.
bullets: Embryos are grown in vitro to the 8-cell stage (or blastocyst).
A single cell is safely removed from each embryo without destroying its developmental potential.
DNA is extracted and tested for the target disease allele.
Only healthy, unaffected embryos are selected for transfer into the uterus.

callouts.p: Genetic testing of embryos produced by IVF to select embryos without specific disease alleles before implantation.

core.p: Carrier testing is offered to individuals with a family history of genetic disorders, or people from specific ethnic groups with a high prevalence of certain recessive conditions, to see if they carry one copy of a recessive disease allele.
bullets: Recessive disorders only cause disease if a person inherits two disease alleles (homozygous recessive).
Carriers are heterozygous; they do not have symptoms themselves but can pass the allele to offspring.
If both partners are carriers, there is a 25% chance per pregnancy of having an affected child.
Results guide family planning and reproductive choices.

callouts.p: Carriers have one normal allele and one disease allele. They are healthy but at risk of having affected children if their partner is also a carrier.

core.h: 7. Ethical, Social, and Economic Issues in Genetic Testing
core.p: Advances in genome understanding and genetic testing raise complex ethical dilemmas. Society must balance the benefits of early medical intervention against privacy risks, discrimination, and emotional distress.
bullets: Discrimination by insurance companies and employers based on genetic test results.
Psychological stress of knowing one carries a predisposition to an incurable disease like Huntington's.
Ethical debates surrounding the termination of pregnancy after prenatal testing or the discarding of embryos in PGD.
Access to genetic testing and personalized medicine across different socio-economic groups.

callouts.p: Do not just state 'ethics' in an exam. You must explain specific ethical issues, such as insurance discrimination, anxiety from predictive tests, or abortion/embryo disposal debates.

core.p: Understanding the genome allows doctors to tailor medical treatments to an individual's specific genetic makeup, a field known as personalised medicine or pharmacogenomics.
bullets: Different genetic variants affect how patients metabolise certain pharmaceutical drugs.
Genetic tests can predict which drug dosage will be most effective and least toxic for a specific patient.
Reduces adverse drug reactions and improves treatment success rates, particularly in cancer therapy.
Identifies target proteins for novel targeted drugs.

callouts.p: Medical treatment tailored to match the specific genetic characteristics and variant profile of an individual patient.

analogy.p: Imagine the human genome is a massive instruction manual for building a car. A disease allele is like a single misprinted instruction in the engine assembly chapter, causing a vital part to be built incorrectly. Genetic testing is like quality control inspecting specific pages of the manual before the car is built (PGD/prenatal) or after it is on the road (diagnostic/predictive) to warn owners of potential breakdowns. Where the analogy breaks down is that cars are mechanical and can be disassembled easily, whereas human gene therapy and multi-factorial disease influences are vastly more complex and interconnected.

terms.d: A variant form of a gene that causes or increases susceptibility to a genetic disorder.
Analysis of human DNA, chromosomes, or proteins to detect disease-causing alleles or variants.
Genetic testing to identify risk of developing a genetic condition later in life before symptoms appear.
Genetic testing used to confirm or rule out a suspected genetic disorder in a symptomatic patient.
Testing fetal cells during pregnancy for genetic conditions using amniocentesis or CVS.
Prenatal test involving extraction of amniotic fluid at 15-20 weeks of pregnancy.
Prenatal test involving extraction of placental tissue at 11-14 weeks of pregnancy.
Genetic screening of embryos created by IVF to select unaffected embryos before implantation.
Genetic testing to determine if an individual carries one copy of a recessive disease allele.
Medical care customized to an individual's genetic profile to optimize drug efficacy and safety.
Having two different alleles for a particular gene.
Conditions controlled by interactions between multiple genes and environmental factors.

mistakes.w: Saying carriers have the disease.
mistakes.r: Carriers have one recessive disease allele and one normal allele, so they are healthy (heterozygous) but can pass the allele on.

mistakes.w: Confusing amniocentesis and CVS timeframes.
mistakes.r: CVS is done earlier (11-14 weeks); amniocentesis is done later (15-20 weeks).

mistakes.w: Stating genetic tests can cure genetic diseases.
mistakes.r: Genetic testing only identifies or diagnoses conditions; it does not cure them.

mistakes.w: Believing a positive predictive test means a person will definitely get the disease.
mistakes.r: Many predictive tests show increased risk or probability, and environmental factors or penetrance play a role.

mistakes.w: Writing that PGD tests adults.
mistakes.r: PGD is performed on early-stage embryos created via IVF.

mistakes.w: Confusing diagnostic and predictive tests.
mistakes.r: Diagnostic tests check patients with current symptoms; predictive tests check healthy people for future risks.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the main risk of invasive prenatal testing.
mistakes.r: Amniocentesis and CVS both carry a small risk of inducing a miscarriage.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a 'disease allele'.
model: An alternative form / variant of a gene
that leads to a faulty protein causing a genetic disorder
exam.tip: Mention both the genetic nature (variant gene) and the functional consequence (faulty protein/disorder).

exam.q: Describe how pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used in fertility treatment.
model: Embryos are created using IVF
A single cell is removed from the embryo at an early stage
DNA is tested for the specific disease allele
Only embryos without the disease allele are selected and implanted into the uterus
exam.tip: Reference IVF, cell removal, testing, and selective implantation in order.

exam.q: Compare amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS) as methods of prenatal testing.
model: CVS is performed earlier in pregnancy (11-14 weeks) than amniocentesis (15-20 weeks)
CVS samples placental tissue whereas amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid
Both methods carry a risk of causing a miscarriage
exam.tip: Make sure you give at least one difference in timing or sample source and one similarity.

exam.q: Discuss one ethical issue surrounding predictive genetic testing for a late-onset inherited disorder like Huntington's disease.
model: Can cause severe psychological distress/anxiety knowing you will develop an incurable disease
May lead to genetic discrimination by insurance companies or employers
Can influence personal life choices such as whether to have children
exam.tip: State the issue clearly and explain the consequence for the individual or society to gain full marks.

exam.q: A couple are both carriers for cystic fibrosis, a recessive genetic disorder. Explain the probability of them having a child with cystic fibrosis.
model: Both parents are heterozygous (e.g., Cc)
Each parent produces 50% normal (C) gametes and 50% disease (c) gametes
Punnet square yields 1 in 4 (25%) chance of homozygous recessive (cc) offspring
Therefore, there is a 25% probability of having an affected child
exam.tip: Use standard genetic terminology: heterozygous, gametes, recessive, and calculate the 25% ratio.

exam.q: State two reasons why someone might choose to undergo carrier testing.
model: To find out if they carry a recessive disease allele before starting a family
To help make informed reproductive or family planning decisions
exam.tip: Keep answers concise and directly related to recessive alleles and family planning.

exam.q: Explain how personalised medicine relies on understanding an individual's genome.
model: Different people have genetic variants that affect how they metabolise medicines
Genetic tests identify these specific variants
Doctors can then select the most effective drug and correct dosage to minimise side effects
exam.tip: Link genetic variation directly to drug metabolism and tailored medical treatment.

exam.q: Describe the difference between diagnostic testing and predictive testing.
model: Diagnostic testing is used to confirm a condition when symptoms are already present
Predictive testing identifies genetic risks in healthy individuals before symptoms appear
exam.tip: Contrast the presence of symptoms in diagnostic testing with the lack of symptoms in predictive testing.

exam.q: Explain why PGD is used instead of natural conception and prenatal testing for some couples.
model: PGD checks embryos before pregnancy is established, avoiding the difficult decision of whether to terminate a pregnancy after prenatal testing
exam.tip: Focus on the avoidance of pregnancy termination as a primary reason for choosing PGD.

worked.q: A genetic counselor calculates that two carrier parents have a 25% chance of having a child with a recessive genetic disorder. If they have 4 children, predict how many will definitely have the disorder.
steps: Identify that each pregnancy is an independent event with a 0.25 (25%) probability.
Multiply the total number of children (4) by the probability (0.25).
Acknowledge that probability does not guarantee exact outcomes in small sample sizes.
worked.ans: Statistically 1 child, but because each birth is an independent event, any number from 0 to 4 is possible in reality.

worked.q: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks gestation is offered prenatal testing. Should she be offered amniocentesis or CVS? Explain your reasoning.
steps: Check the gestational age given in the question: 12 weeks.
Compare with the timeframes for both tests: CVS is 11-14 weeks, amniocentesis is 15-20 weeks.
Conclude which test is appropriate.
worked.ans: She should be offered CVS because it is performed between 11 and 14 weeks, whereas amniocentesis is not performed until 15 to 20 weeks.

bio_ocrb.0.10.summary: Genetic engineering is the deliberate modification of an organism's genome by inserting a gene from another organism to achieve a desired characteristic. This complex process involves using specific enzymes to cut and paste DNA, employing vectors like plasmids to transport genetic material, and utilizing marker genes to identify which cells have successfully taken up the new instructions. By bypassing traditional breeding, scientists can create transgenic organisms that produce human proteins, resist pests, or survive harsh environmental conditions.

core.p: Genetic engineering (GE) involves changing the DNA of an organism by inserting a gene from another species. This creates a **transgenic organism** or a **Genetically Modified Organism (GMO)**. Unlike selective breeding, which works with existing alleles within a species, GE allows for the transfer of specific traits across different kingdoms of life, such as putting human genes into bacteria.
bullets: The organism receiving the gene is the **host**.
The organism providing the gene is the **donor**.
The resulting DNA is called **recombinant DNA**.
The process is rapid compared to traditional breeding methods.

callouts.p: A process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.

core.p: The first step is to identify and 'cut out' the specific gene responsible for the desired trait from the donor's DNA. This is done using specialized proteins called **restriction enzymes**.
bullets: Restriction enzymes recognize specific sequences of DNA bases.
They cut the DNA at these specific points, leaving staggered ends.
These staggered ends are called **sticky ends** because they have exposed unpaired bases.
Sticky ends are crucial because they will only bind to complementary sequences cut by the same enzyme.

core.p: Once isolated, the gene must be copied many times to ensure there is enough material for the engineering process. This is often done using a technique called **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**.
bullets: PCR uses a heat-stable DNA polymerase enzyme.
The DNA is heated to separate strands and cooled to allow primers to bind.
This allows for exponential amplification of the specific gene sequence.
In OCR exams, this is often referred to as 'replicating the gene' before insertion.

core.h: Step 3: Choosing and Preparing a Vector
core.p: A **vector** is a carrier used to transfer the isolated gene into the host cell. The most common vectors are **plasmids** and **viruses**.
bullets: **Plasmids**: Small, circular loops of extra-chromosomal DNA found in bacteria.
**Viruses**: Can naturally inject their genetic material into host cells.
The vector is cut open using the **same restriction enzyme** used to isolate the gene.
Using the same enzyme ensures the vector has sticky ends that are complementary to the gene's sticky ends.

callouts.p: You must use the same restriction enzyme for both the gene and the vector so the sticky ends match perfectly (complementary base pairing).

core.p: The isolated gene and the opened vector are mixed together. Because their sticky ends are complementary, they join via base pairing. However, the sugar-phosphate backbone is still broken.
bullets: An enzyme called **DNA ligase** is added to the mixture.
Ligase acts like 'biological glue', joining the DNA strands together.
This forms a single, continuous loop of **recombinant DNA**.
The vector now contains the instructions to produce the new protein.

core.h: Step 5: Inserting the Vector into the Host
core.p: The recombinant vector must now be placed into the host cells (e.g., bacteria or plant cells). This process is called **transformation**.
bullets: Bacteria are often shocked (using heat or electricity) to make their cell membranes more permeable.
This allows the plasmid to enter the bacterial cell.
If a virus is used, it simply 'infects' the host cell, injecting the recombinant DNA.
Not every cell will successfully take up the vector; this is a low-efficiency process.

core.p: Since many host cells fail to take up the vector, scientists must identify and 'select' only the successfully modified cells. This is achieved using **marker genes**.
bullets: A marker gene (often for **antibiotic resistance**) is included in the vector alongside the desired gene.
The host cells are grown on agar plates containing the specific antibiotic.
Cells that did NOT take up the plasmid will die because they lack the resistance gene.
Only the successfully modified (transformed) cells survive and grow into colonies.

fig.cap: Selection process: Only bacteria containing the recombinant plasmid (with the antibiotic resistance marker) can grow on the antibiotic-treated agar.

core.p: Once the modified cells are selected, they are allowed to multiply. In the case of bacteria, they divide rapidly by **binary fission**.
bullets: As the bacteria replicate, they also replicate the recombinant plasmid.
Every daughter cell now contains the new gene.
The bacteria 'read' the gene and produce the desired protein (e.g., insulin) through protein synthesis.
The protein is then extracted and purified for human use.

core.p: Two main enzymes are the 'tools' of the genetic engineer. Understanding their distinct roles is vital for exam success.

core.p: Before GE, insulin for diabetics was extracted from the pancreases of slaughtered pigs and cows. GE changed this.
bullets: The human insulin gene is isolated from human DNA.
It is inserted into a bacterial plasmid.
The recombinant bacteria are grown in large industrial **fermenters**.
The bacteria produce 'human' insulin, which is chemically identical to that made in a healthy human pancreas.
This reduces the risk of allergic reactions and is more ethical for many people.

core.p: GE is widely used in agriculture to create crops that can survive being sprayed with weed-killers (herbicides).
bullets: A gene for herbicide resistance is isolated from a soil bacterium.
The gene is inserted into the genome of crop plants like maize or soy.
Farmers can spray their entire field with herbicide; the weeds die, but the GM crops survive.
This increases crop yield by reducing competition for light and nutrients.

callouts.p: A major concern is that these resistance genes could spread to wild plants (weeds) via cross-pollination, creating 'superweeds'.

core.p: To master this topic, you must be able to sequence the steps correctly from start to finish.

analogy.p: Imagine the DNA of every living thing is a recipe book. Genetic engineering is like finding a specific recipe for 'Perfect Chocolate Frosting' in a French cookbook (the donor), using a pair of scissors (restriction enzymes) to cut it out, and then using tape (ligase) to paste it into an English baking book (the host). Now, the English book can produce the frosting. The analogy breaks down because in biology, the 'tape' must be a specific chemical bond, and you need a 'delivery truck' (vector) to get the recipe into the new kitchen, which might reject it if you don't use a 'secret code' (marker gene) to prove it belongs there.

An enzyme used to join two DNA fragments together.
A mechanism (like a plasmid or virus) used to carry a gene into a host cell.

mistakes.w: Restriction enzymes melt the hydrogen bonds in DNA.
mistakes.r: Restriction enzymes break the chemical bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA.

mistakes.w: Plasmids are found in the nucleus of bacteria.
mistakes.r: Bacteria are prokaryotes and do not have a nucleus; plasmids are found in the cytoplasm.

mistakes.w: You use different enzymes to cut the gene and the plasmid.
mistakes.r: You must use the same restriction enzyme so that the sticky ends are complementary.

mistakes.w: Ligase cuts the DNA.
mistakes.r: Ligase joins (ligates) DNA fragments; restriction enzymes do the cutting.

mistakes.w: All bacteria take up the plasmid during transformation.
mistakes.r: Transformation is inefficient; only a small percentage of bacteria successfully take up the plasmid.

mistakes.w: Genetic engineering is the same as selective breeding.
mistakes.r: GE involves direct lab manipulation of DNA across species; selective breeding uses natural reproduction within a species.

mistakes.w: The marker gene is the gene we want to use (e.g. insulin).
mistakes.r: The marker gene is an extra gene (like antibiotic resistance) used only to identify successful cells.

mistakes.w: Viruses are the only vectors used.
mistakes.r: Plasmids are the most common vectors, though viruses are also used.

exam.q: Define the term 'vector' in the context of genetic engineering.
model: A vehicle or carrier used to transfer genetic material/DNA into a host cell.
exam.tip: Don't confuse this with vectors in physics or disease vectors (like mosquitoes)!

exam.q: Explain why it is essential to use the same restriction enzyme to cut both the desired gene and the plasmid vector.
model: To ensure the sticky ends produced are complementary to each other.
This allows the bases on the sticky ends to pair up/join via hydrogen bonding.
exam.tip: The word 'complementary' is a high-scoring keyword here.

exam.q: State the role of DNA ligase in the production of recombinant DNA.
model: It joins the sugar-phosphate backbones of the gene and the vector together.
exam.tip: Think of ligase as the 'glue'.

exam.q: Describe how scientists can identify which bacteria have successfully taken up a recombinant plasmid.
model: A marker gene for antibiotic resistance is added to the plasmid.
Bacteria are grown on agar containing that antibiotic.
Only the bacteria with the plasmid will survive and grow.
exam.tip: Mentioning 'antibiotic resistance' is the standard example for marker genes.

exam.q: Give two advantages of producing insulin using genetic engineering rather than extracting it from animals.
model: It is identical to human insulin so there is no risk of allergic reaction.
It can be produced in large quantities more cheaply/efficiently.
It avoids ethical/religious concerns regarding the use of animal products.
exam.tip: Any two of these will get the marks.

exam.q: Suggest one risk associated with the use of genetically modified herbicide-resistant crops.
model: The resistance gene could transfer to wild plants/weeds (creating superweeds).
exam.tip: Focus on the biological/environmental risk.

exam.q: What are 'sticky ends'?
model: Short lengths of single-stranded DNA.
Found at the ends of a DNA fragment after being cut by a restriction enzyme.
exam.tip: Be specific about them being single-stranded.

exam.q: Outline the steps involved in replicating a gene once it has been isolated.
model: The gene is copied using PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction).
Or the gene is inserted into a bacterium which then replicates through cell division.
exam.tip: Both methods are technically correct for 'replicating' the gene.

exam.q: Explain the process of genetic engineering to produce a transgenic plant. (6 marks)
model: Identify the desired gene in the donor organism.
Cut out the gene using a specific restriction enzyme to create sticky ends.
Use the same restriction enzyme to cut open a vector (e.g., a plasmid or Agrobacterium).
Join the gene and vector using DNA ligase to create recombinant DNA.
Insert the vector into the plant cells (transformation).
Use a marker gene to select the cells that have successfully taken up the new DNA.
Grow the modified cells into whole plants using tissue culture.
exam.tip: For 6 marks, you must sequence the steps logically and use the correct enzyme names.

worked.q: A scientist wants to insert a gene for vitamin A production into rice. The gene sequence has the restriction site 'GAATTC'. Which enzyme should they use to cut the rice DNA, and what must they do to the vector?
steps: Identify the restriction enzyme that recognizes 'GAATTC' (EcoRI).
Apply this enzyme to the donor DNA to isolate the vitamin A gene.
Apply the EXACT SAME enzyme to the vector DNA.
This ensures the sticky ends on the rice gene and the vector are complementary (e.g., AATT matches TTAA).
worked.ans: They must use the restriction enzyme EcoRI (or the one specific to that sequence) on both the donor DNA and the vector to create matching sticky ends.

worked.q: In a lab, 1000 bacterial cells were treated with a recombinant plasmid containing an ampicillin-resistance marker. After plating on ampicillin-agar, only 15 colonies grew. Calculate the efficiency of the transformation as a percentage.
steps: Efficiency = (Number of successful cells / Total number of cells) x 100
Efficiency = (15 / 1000) x 100
Efficiency = 0.015 x 100
